You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current approaches to Zero-Shot Skeleton-based Action Recognition (ZSSAR) suffer from a reliance on rigid, manually crafted constraints. Existing methods attempt to bridge the gap between visual skeleton data and unseen action labels by using hand-engineered descriptions (e.g., "verb+noun" rules) or GPT-generated sentences. These manual interventions are often brittle, noisy, and lack flexibility.

Furthermore, attempts to adapt powerful Vision-Language Models (like CLIP) to this domain via standard prompt learning face two critical hurdles:
1.  **Catastrophic Distortion:** Training learnable prompts on "seen" classes alters the model's internal attention mechanisms, causing it to overfit and lose the pre-trained generalization capability required for "unseen" classes.
2.  **Structural Mismatch:** Standard visual prompting techniques designed for 2D image grids are incompatible with the sparse, graph-like structure of 3D skeleton joint sequences.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can achieve robust zero-shot generalization without manual semantic engineering by implementing a **dual-stream** prompting strategy. Our core insight is that optimal adaptation requires a balance: we must explicitly preserve the original pre-trained semantic context (to maintain generalizability) while simultaneously learning task-specific adjustments (to handle domain shifts).

Additionally, we propose that effective visual prompting for skeletons requires prompts that mimic the native data structure. By treating prompts as "virtual joints" and guiding them via textual semantics, we can align disparate modalities more effectively than through static feature projection.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a Semantic-guided Cross-Modal Prompt Learning framework. The approach focuses on purely data-driven tuning across two aligned branches:

**1. Dual-Stream Language Prompting (DSLP)**
Instead of simply modifying the input to a text encoder, we propose a parallel processing architecture within the Transformer layers:
*   **Frozen Stream:** The first stream processes the original action labels using the frozen pre-trained weights. This preserves the "authentic" semantic context and attention distribution of the foundation model.
*   **Prompted Stream:** The second stream incorporates learnable layer-level prompts to tune features for the specific action recognition task.
*   **Fusion Logic:** Crucially, we will implement a mechanism that dynamically aggregates attention outputs from the Frozen Stream into the Prompted Stream. This acts as a regularizer, ensuring the learnable prompts refine the features without destroying the semantic structure necessary for recognizing unseen classes.

**2. Semantic-Guided Skeleton Prompting**
We aim to introduce prompt learning to the visual (skeleton) backbone in a structure-aware manner:
*   **Joint-Shaped Prompts:** We will initialize learnable vectors that match the dimension and shape of actual body joint features. These "virtual joints" will be appended to the input sequence, allowing the graph convolution backbone to process them alongside real data.
*   **Adaptive Visual Sampler:** To align these skeleton features with the text, we will design a cross-attention sampler. In this module, the text embeddings (from the DSLP module) will act as *queries*. These queries will attend to the skeleton features (keys/values) to dynamically weigh and select the specific body joints—or virtual prompt joints—that are most relevant to the current semantic context.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical:** We aim to demonstrate that preserving the attention distribution of the original pre-trained model is the key factor in stabilizing prompt learning for zero-shot tasks, solving the issue where adapting to "seen" classes degrades "unseen" performance.
*   **Methodological:** We will provide a novel prompting paradigm for non-image 3D data, showing how to implement "structure-aware" prompts (joint-shaped) rather than generic patch-based prompts.
*   **Practical:** The proposed framework will eliminate the need for labor-intensive manual descriptions or external knowledge bases in ZSSAR, establishing a fully automated, data-driven pipeline.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a rigorous experimental framework to evaluate the proposed Semantic-guided Cross-Modal Prompt Learning (SCoPLe) method for Zero-Shot Skeleton-Based Action Recognition (ZSSAR) and Generalized ZSSAR (GZSSAR).

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **NTU-RGB+D 60:** Contains 56,880 video samples, 60 action classes, 40 subjects, 80 viewpoints. Skeleton sequences used 25 body joints (2 performers).
        *   *Evaluation Splits:* 55/5 split (55 seen, 5 unseen classes) and 48/12 split.
    *   **NTU-RGB+D 120:** Contains 114,480 samples, 120 classes, 106 subjects, 155 viewpoints.
        *   *Evaluation Splits:* 110/10 split and 96/24 split.
    *   **PKU-MMD:** Contains 51 action categories, over 20,000 instances. Evaluated on interaction and group activities.
        *   *Evaluation Splits:* Calculated average accuracy from three random split settings in the format of 46/5.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL):** Top-1 Accuracy (%) for unseen classes.
    *   **Generalized Zero-Shot Learning (GZSL):**
        *   **S:** Accuracy on Seen classes.
        *   **U:** Accuracy on Unseen classes.
        *   **H:** Harmonic mean of S and U (main metric for GZSL).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Language/Skeleton Baselines:** ReViSE, JPoSE, CADA-VAE, SynSE, SMIE, STAR, PURLS, SA-DVAE.
    *   **CLIP Adaptations:** CLIP (vanilla), CLIP-CoOp, CLIP-MaPLe.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Backbones:** Shift-GCN (skeleton visual backbone, pre-trained on seen classes), CLIP-ViT-B/32 (text backbone, frozen weights).
    *   **Feature Dimensions:** Skeleton features ($d_{skel}$) = 256; Textual features ($F$) = 512.
    *   **Projection:** Two-layer MLP with SiLU activations and Tanh output. Hidden layer size = 512.
    *   **Hyperparameters:**
        *   Prefix prompt length ($P^{\mathcal{T}}_0$): 2.
        *   Layer prompt tuning depth ($S$): 3.
        *   Number of joint-shaped prompts ($L_{Pv}$): 3.
        *   Initialization: Random normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ for layer-level prompts.
        *   Mixing parameter $\alpha_s$: Initialized to 0.5.
    *   **Training Configuration:**
        *   Hardware: Single A100 GPU.
        *   Framework: PyTorch.
        *   Epochs: 100.
        *   Batch Size: 256.
        *   Optimizer: Adam ($\beta_1=0.9, \beta_2=0.999$).
        *   Learning Rate: $1e-4$.
    *   **GZSL Inference Strategy:** Employed an entropy-based gating mechanism with a threshold $\delta$ to distinguish between seen and unseen classes before classification.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

Based on our analysis of the experimental process and visual data, we recorded the following observations:

*   **Architecture Observation (Visual vs. Textual Tuning):** We implemented a Dual-Stream Language Prompting (DSLP) module. One stream preserved original pre-trained CLIP knowledge, while the second stream utilized layer-level prompts. We observed that this design effectively normalized textual prompt learning compared to single-stream approaches.
*   **Architecture Observation (Skeleton Prompting):** We utilized "joint-shaped prompts"—fake joint features initialized randomly ($N(0,1)$)—combined with real skeleton features. This structure was specifically compatible with the Shift-GCN backbone input format.
*   **Mechanism Observation (Visual Sampler):** The Adaptive Visual Representation Sampler used the textual embeddings (queries) to sample from the skeleton features (keys/values). We observed that this allowed the model to highlight class-relevant visual contexts dynamically based on the label.
*   **Hyperparameter Sensitivity (Prefix Prompt Length):** We conducted a grid search on the prefix prompt length ($P_0^{\mathcal{T}}$). Performance improved as length increased from 0 to 2, peaking at 2. Performance degraded for lengths greater than 2, suggesting overfitting.
*   **Hyperparameter Sensitivity (Layer Prompt Depth):** We varied the number of prompted layers ($S$). Accuracy peaked at $S=3$. Deeper prompting (values 5, 7, 9, 11) led to a gradual decline in accuracy.
*   **Hyperparameter Sensitivity (Joint Prompt Number):** We varied the number of fake joint prompts ($L_{Pv}$). Performance was optimal at 3 prompts. Increasing the number beyond 3 resulted in decreased accuracy.
*   **Ablation Observation (Prompting Types):** We observed that removing all prompts (reverting to standard CLIP) drastically reduced performance. Furthermore, removing text prompts while keeping skeleton prompts resulted in unstable advancement, indicating ZSL relies heavily on high-quality language embeddings.
*   **Ablation Observation (Dual-Stream):** Comparing "no dual" to the full model, we observed that the dual-stream normalization improved the balance between seen and unseen class prediction accuracy in Generalized ZSSAR scenarios.
*   **Training Efficiency:** We compared training time on the NTU-120 (110/10 split) against the PURLS baseline. Our method required 53 minutes, whereas PURLS required 72 minutes, demonstrating improved efficiency.
*   **Base-to-Novel Generalization:** While the primary focus was skeleton data, preliminary exploration suggested the fully data-driven prompt modules theoretically support extension to other modalities like image-based tasks.

# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Current approaches to Zero-Shot Skeleton-Based Action Recognition (ZSSAR) face a critical bottleneck: they rely heavily on manual semantic engineering. Existing methods bridge the gap between visual skeleton data and textual labels by utilizing handcrafted action descriptions, "verb+noun" decomposition, or auxiliary text generated by Large Language Models (e.g., GPT). These manual interventions introduce noise, lack flexibility, and impose rigid assumptions that do not scale to complex, unseen action categories.

Furthermore, while prompt learning has revolutionized image-text models (like CLIP), directly applying existing prompting techniques (e.g., CoOp, MaPLe) to ZSSAR is suboptimal. Standard prompt learning tends to over-optimize the text encoder for "seen" classes, distorting the pre-trained attention distribution and compromising the model's inherent ability to generalize to "unseen" classes. Additionally, standard visual prompting techniques designed for grid-based images are incompatible with the graph-structured nature of skeleton data ($L \times J \times M \times 3$), leaving the visual branch unadapted.

## Core Hypothesis

We hypothesize that we can achieve superior ZSSAR performance without manual semantic crafting by implementing a fully data-driven **Semantic-guided Cross-Modal Prompt Learning (SCoPLe)** framework.

Our core technical hypotheses are:
1.  **Dual-Stream Text Integrity:** By decoupling prompt tuning from the original semantic context via a **Dual-Stream Language Prompting (DSLP)** module, we can tune features for the specific task while forcing the model to retain the generalization capability of the frozen pre-trained weights.
2.  **Skeleton-Aware Visual Prompting:** We can introduce "visual prompts" as learnable "fake joints" within the skeleton graph. By employing an **Adaptive Visual Representation Sampler**, we can use the text embeddings to actively query and weight these skeleton features, ensuring that the visual representation is dynamically aligned with the semantic context of the action label.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will construct a cross-modal alignment framework consisting of a frozen Shift-GCN skeleton encoder and a frozen CLIP text encoder, augmented by our proposed learnable prompting modules.

### 1. Problem Formulation
We define the training set $\mathcal{D}_{tr} = \{(x_{tr}^{sc}, y_{tr}^{sc})\}$ containing $N_{tr}$ samples from seen classes $\mathcal{V}^{sc}$. The input $x$ is a skeleton sequence $x \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times J \times M \times 3}$, representing $L$ frames, $J$ joints, $M$ actors, and 3D coordinates. The test set $\mathcal{D}_{te}$ contains samples from unseen classes $\mathcal{V}^{uc}$, where $\mathcal{V}^{sc} \cap \mathcal{V}^{uc} = \emptyset$.

### 2. Dual-Stream Language Prompting (DSLP)
To adapt the CLIP text encoder $\tau$ without losing its generalization capabilities, we will modify the first $S$ transformer layers to process two parallel streams: an **original encoding stream** and a **prompted encoding stream**.

**Input Construction:**
We will initialize a preamble prompt: "A skeleton video for the action of [LABEL]". We will replace the first two tokens with a learnable vector $P_0^{\mathcal{T}}$. The input to the text encoder is denoted as $E_0$.

**Layer-wise Processing:**
For a given layer $\mathcal{T}_s$, we process two inputs: $E_{s-1}$ (original stream) and $E'_{s-1}$ (prompted stream).

The **original stream** computes the standard self-attention output $\hat{E}_s$ to preserve authentic semantics:
$$
\hat{E}_s = \mathrm{Att}_s(\mathrm{LayerNorm}(E_{s-1}))
$$

The **prompted stream** incorporates a layer-specific learnable prompt $P_s^{\mathcal{T}}$. We define $E_{s-1}^*$ as the prompted input where specific token positions are replaced by $P_s^{\mathcal{T}}$. Crucially, we will implement a weighted aggregation mechanism that injects the attention pattern from the *original* stream into the prompted stream to maintain structural integrity. The fused input $E_{s-1}^{**}$ is calculated as:
$$
E_{s-1}^{**} = (1 - \alpha_s)E_{s-1}^* + \alpha_s \hat{E}_s
$$
where $\alpha_s$ is a learnable parameter initialized to balance tuning and preservation. This fused input then passes through the standard layer operations (Attention and FFN) to produce $E'_s$.

The final textual embedding $F \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{text}}$ is obtained by passing the output of the $S$-th prompted layer through the remaining frozen layers of $\tau$.

### 3. Semantic-Guided Skeleton Prompting
On the visual side, we will introduce a prompting mechanism tailored to the graph structure of skeleton data.

**Joint-Shaped Prompts:**
We extract initial visual features $G = \mathcal{G}(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{J \times d_{skel}}$ using the frozen backbone. We will define visual prompts $P^{\nu} \in \mathbb{R}^{L_P \nu \times d_{skel}}$ as a set of $L_P \nu$ learnable vectors. Structurally, these will act as "fake joints" appended to the skeleton feature graph.

**Adaptive Visual Representation Sampler:**
To align skeleton features with text semantics, we will implement a cross-attention mechanism where the text embedding acts as the query. We define three learnable projection matrices: $\mathbf{W}_Q$, $\mathbf{W}_K$, and $\mathbf{W}_V$.

We compute the query $F_Q$, and the key/value pairs ($G_K, G_V$) from the concatenation of prompts $P^{\nu}$ and skeleton features $G$:
$$
\begin{array} { r l }
F_Q & = F \mathbf{W}_Q \\
G_K & = [P^{\nu}, G] \mathbf{W}_K \\
G_V & = [P^{\nu}, G] \mathbf{W}_V
\end{array}
$$
We calculate the relevance score $A$ and the final visual representation $R$:
$$
A = \mathrm{Softmax}\left( \frac{F_Q \times G_K^T}{\sqrt{h}} \right)
$$
$$
R = A G_V
$$
Finally, $R$ is projected via an MLP $\nu$ to the visual embedding $V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{text}}$.

### 4. Learning Objective
We will train the prompting parameters (while keeping backbones frozen) using a standard contrastive loss to maximize the similarity between matched visual-text pairs:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{train}(V, F) = - \frac{1}{2} \log \frac{\exp(V \cdot F / \tau)}{\sum_{o} \exp(V \cdot F_o / \tau)} - \frac{1}{2} \log \frac{\exp(V \cdot F / \tau)}{\sum_{w} \exp(V_w \cdot F / \tau)}
$$
where $\tau$ is the temperature parameter, $F_o$ represents negative text samples, and $V_w$ represents negative visual samples in the batch.

### 5. Generalized ZSSAR Inference Strategy
For Generalized ZSSAR (identifying both seen and unseen classes), we will implement an entropy-based gating mechanism. We calculate the prediction entropy $H_y$ over the seen classes. If $H_y$ is below a threshold $\delta$, we classify the sample as a "seen" class; otherwise, we classify it as an "unseen" class.

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Elimination of Manual Engineering:** We provide a methodology that removes the need for handcrafted attributes, descriptions, or complex semantic decomposition in ZSSAR.
2.  **Preservation of Generalization:** The Dual-Stream Language Prompting design theoretically resolves the trade-off between task adaptation and the catastrophic forgetting of open-world knowledge in pre-trained models.
3.  **Skeleton-Specific Alignment:** By formulating visual prompts as "fake joints" and employing text-guided sampling, we offer a novel mechanism for aligning graph-structured data with linguistic semantics, contributing a new architectural primitive for multi-modal skeleton analysis.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.

notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.

notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
